items.paragraph: A familiar argument holds that any resource open to all, such as a pasture, a fishery or a forest, will be overused until it is ruined, because each user gains the full benefit of taking more while the cost is shared by everyone. The only remedies, on this view, are private ownership or control by the state. The argument is sound for resources that truly are open to anyone, but many traditional commons were nothing of the kind. Villages that shared grazing land or irrigation water often had detailed rules about who could use the resource, how much and when, together with ways of watching for cheaters and punishing them. Such arrangements have kept some resources in good condition for centuries. They do not always work, and they tend to fail when outsiders arrive or when the community loses its authority, but they show that the choice is not limited to the market or the state.

items.paragraph: Campaigns to purify a language usually begin from the fear that borrowed words are a kind of erosion, each foreign term a small loss of the native stock. The fear misdescribes how languages grow. A borrowed word rarely displaces an existing one outright; more often it settles beside it and the two divide the territory, one taking a formal shade and the other an everyday one, so that the language ends up able to say more rather than less. Borrowing is also old: most languages that purists wish to protect were themselves assembled from earlier contacts. None of this means that every borrowing is welcome or that speakers cannot reasonably prefer a native coinage. It means that the decision is one of taste, not a defence against decay.

options.B: Residents who do not own cars pay more for their flats, because developers are forced to build parking spaces that only car-owning residents will ever actually use.
options.C: Cities should ban new parking spaces altogether, because parking uses up land and money and tempts people to drive when they could walk or take public transport instead.
options.D: Required parking raises building costs for drivers and non-drivers alike and encourages driving, so though some parking is needed, its amount should not be set by rule.

items.paragraph: Many cities require every new building to provide a minimum number of parking spaces, a rule meant to stop drivers from overwhelming the surrounding streets. The intention is sensible, but the rule carries costs that are easy to overlook because they are hidden in other prices. Parking takes land and money, so the requirement raises the cost of every flat and shop that is built, whether or not its occupants own a car; residents who do not drive in effect subsidise those who do. And by guaranteeing that driving will always be convenient, the rule encourages more of it, partly creating the demand it was meant to accommodate. None of this means a city should have no parking. It means that the amount should be decided by those who build and use it, rather than fixed by a rule that assumes everyone will drive.

options.A: Because forest storage is reversible while fossil carbon persists, an offset is a delay whose value depends on secure storage, not a cancellation of the emission.
options.B: Because trees can burn or be felled, forest offsets do nothing to address emissions, and they should be abandoned in favour of directly cutting the use of fossil fuel.
options.C: The weakness of forest offsets lies in measurement, since the carbon held in trees cannot be counted as accurately as the carbon released when fuel is burned.
options.D: Forest offsets are valuable chiefly because they buy time, so a tonne of carbon stored in trees should be counted as equal to a tonne released by burning fuel.

items.paragraph: An offset that pays to plant a forest is often treated as cancelling an equivalent quantity of emissions from a flight or a factory. The equivalence is only arithmetical. Carbon released from burning fossil fuel stays in the atmosphere for centuries, while carbon stored in trees is held only as long as the trees survive fire, disease, drought and the decisions of future landowners. The two quantities are measured in the same tonnes, yet one is a near-permanent addition and the other a reversible loan. None of this means that planting forests is worthless; a stored tonne buys time, and time has value. It means that an offset should be counted as a delay whose worth depends on how securely the storage can be guaranteed, rather than as an erasure that lets the original emission be forgotten.

items.paragraph: Satellite navigation has made it hard to get lost in an unfamiliar city. (1) A voice announces each turn shortly before it arrives, and the driver need only follow. (2) People who navigate by spoken instructions tend to form a poorer picture of the area they have passed through than people who have worked out the route for themselves. They may reach the destination without being able to say in which direction it lay or how it related to places they already knew. (3) For most journeys this hardly matters. It matters a good deal when the signal fails, the battery dies or the device sends the driver down a road that has been closed. (4) A traveller who glances at the whole map before setting out, and checks it against the streets now and then, can keep most of the convenience while holding on to some of the old skill.

options.A: Speakers who move easily between dialect and standard show that regional dialects face no real threat from schools or from any other source.
options.B: Children who are told that their way of speaking is wrong tend to believe it and may then give up the dialect they first learned at home.
options.C: Teaching a standard variety need not erase dialects, since people can use both; what endangers dialects is treating them as errors rather than as varieties.
options.D: Schools should stop teaching the standard form of the language, because doing so inevitably destroys the regional dialects that pupils bring with them from home.

items.paragraph: Schools that teach a standard form of a language are sometimes accused of destroying the regional dialects their pupils bring from home. The charge contains a truth: children who are told that their way of speaking is wrong often come to feel that it is, and may abandon it. But the fault lies in the telling, not in the teaching of the standard itself. Learning a second variety of one's language, useful in examinations, offices and correspondence with strangers, need not displace the first, any more than learning a second language erases one's mother tongue. Many speakers move between dialect and standard with ease, choosing according to company. What threatens a dialect is the attitude that treats it as a mistake, not the addition of another way of speaking.
